Empirical Research Plan: “The Impact of the 1973-78 INPRES Primary-School Construction Program on Schooling and Adult Earnings of Indonesian Men”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy Two-way difference-in-differences (DID) with continuous treatment intensity; supplemented by an event-study (cohort leads/lags) and a 2SLS “first-stage/returns-to-schooling” exercise that instruments individual schooling with INPRES exposure.  

Why suitable  
• Time dimension: cohorts young enough to attend the new schools vs. cohorts already past primary-school age.  
• Cross-section: districts that received many vs. few schools, with allocation driven by pre-program enrollment (a predetermined rule).  
• Rapid, nation-wide rollout tied to an exogenous oil-revenue shock limits strategic behavior.  
DID therefore cleanly compares changes across cohorts within districts with differing program intensity, purging time-invariant district factors and cohort-invariant national shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable Intensity_d ≡ (# INPRES schools built 1973-78 in district d) ÷ (1971 district population aged 7-12). Scale to “schools per 1,000 children.”  
Treatment cohorts Birth years 1968-72 (ages 2-6 in 1974 → fully exposed when they entered Grade 1).  
Control cohorts Birth years 1950-62 (ages ≥12 in 1974 → too old to benefit). Cohorts 1963-67 (ages 7-11 in 1974) are “partially treated”; include them only in event-study graphs or robustness checks.  
DID variable Post_c = 1 if cohort c ∈ {1968-72}; 0 otherwise.  
Main interaction Treat_icd = Post_c × Intensity_d.  
Counterfactual Older cohorts in high- and low-intensity districts provide the within-district trend; younger cohorts in low-intensity districts provide the cross-section.  
Timing Construction 1973-78; exposure assumed to start with first year of entry (1974).  
(We are not using RDD, so no running variable/cutoff.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1. Parallel trends In the absence of INPRES, the difference in outcomes between high- and low-intensity districts would have evolved similarly across cohorts.  
Plausibility: Allocation rule (low initial enrollment) is time-invariant; oil-revenue shock was nationwide. Event-study on pre-program cohorts can test.  

A2. No differential migration by cohort × intensity Families did not sort across districts in response to the program in a way correlated with potential outcomes.  
Plausibility: Program announced and built quickly; primary-school quality poorly known ex-ante; Indonesia had low inter-district migration in the 1970s. Residual concern addressed by using district of birth (not residence) and testing mobility rates.  

A3. Stable composition (SUTVA/no spillovers) School construction in district d affects only individuals born there; cross-district spillovers are minimal.  
Plausibility: Primary schools serve local catchment areas and travel costs were high in 1970s Indonesia. We will test robustness by dropping bordering districts.  

A4. No other policy differentially correlated with Intensity_d × Post_c.  
Plausibility: The contemporaneous junior-secondary program started later (1980s); public-health campaigns were national. We will control for district-specific linear cohort trends and province-year expenditures.  

A5. Accurate measurement of Intensity_d and cohorts.  
Plausibility: School counts come from official records; birth cohorts self-reported in the 1995 SUPAS and verified via heaping checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats and Mitigations
T1. Pre-program trends in high- vs. low-enrollment districts.  
  Mitigation: (i) Plot event-study coefficients for cohorts born 1950-62 (placebo); expect flat line. (ii) Include district-specific linear trends as robustness.  

T2. Selective migration or measurement using current residence instead of birth.  
  Mitigation: SUPAS reports district of birth—use that. Also replicate with district of 12-year residence to see if results change. Show that migration rates are unrelated to Intensity_d.  

T3. Concurrent investments (roads, health clinics) that also targeted low-enrollment districts.  
  Mitigation: Collect data on INPRES road & health sub-programs; include their intensity as controls. Alternatively, difference-out province-year fixed effects and interact baseline covariates with cohort dummies (à la Bleakley & Ferrie).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # regressions with FEs
library(ggplot2)        # plots

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data -----------------------------------------------
supas   <- fread("supas1995_men1950_1972.csv")     # individual data
schools <- fread("inpres_schoolcounts_1973_78.csv")# district-level
enroll  <- fread("enrollment1971.csv")             # baseline rates

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Construct Variables -----------------------------
# Merge district-level info into individual file
supas <- merge(supas, schools, by = "district_id")
supas <- merge(supas, enroll , by = "district_id")

# Scale treatment intensity (schools per 1,000 children 7-12 in 1971)
supas[, intensity := 1000 * inpres_schools / pop_7_12_1971]

# Create cohort & post indicators
supas[, birthyear := as.integer(birth_year)]
supas[, cohort   := factor(birthyear)]
supas[, post     := fifelse(birthyear >= 1968 & birthyear <= 1972, 1L, 0L)]

# DID interaction
supas[, treat := post * intensity]

# Control variables
supas[, age95   := 1995 - birthyear]
supas[, controls := .(urban, father_edu, mother_edu)] # example

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Regressions ----------------------------------------
# (a) Outcome: years of schooling
did_edu <- feols(years_schooling ~ treat + post + intensity |
                 district_id + cohort,
                 data = supas, cluster = ~district_id)

# (b) Outcome: log real wage
did_wage <- feols(log_wage ~ treat + post + intensity |
                  district_id + cohort,
                  data = supas[employed==1], cluster = ~district_id)

# Print summaries
etable(did_edu, did_wage, se = "cluster")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event Study (visual pre-trend check) --------------------
# Build relative-cohort dummies (k = -18,…,0,…,4; 0 = 1968 cohort)
supas[, rel_cohort := birthyear - 1968]
for(k in -18:4){
  supas[, paste0("D",k) := fifelse(rel_cohort==k, intensity, 0)]
}
fml <- as.formula(paste("years_schooling ~",
            paste0("D", -18:4, collapse="+"), "| district_id + cohort"))
es <- feols(fml, data = supas, cluster = ~district_id)

# Plot coefficients
es_coef <- data.frame(k = -18:4,
                      beta = coef(es)[1:23],
                      se   = se(es)[1:23])
ggplot(es_coef[k<= -6], aes(k,beta)) +          # pre-program window
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=beta-1.96*se, ymax=beta+1.96*se))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype="dashed")+
  theme_bw() + labs(x="Cohort relative to 1968", y="β_k")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: District-Specific Linear Trends -------------
did_trend <- feols(years_schooling ~ treat + post + intensity |
                   district_id[cohort] + cohort,
                   data = supas, cluster = ~district_id)
etable(did_edu, did_trend)
```

Notes  
• Cluster at district level to address within-district serial correlation.  
• For 2SLS: first stage feols(years_schooling ~ treat … ) ‑> second stage feols(log_wage ~ fhat … ).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
Direction Positive: more schools → higher completed grades and higher adult wages.  
Magnitude (priors)  
• Schooling: roughly 0.12–0.15 additional years of education per additional school per 1,000 children (≈ 0.3 SD of intensity). For a district at the 75th vs. 25th percentile of intensity (≈ 2 schools/1,000 difference) that implies ~0.25 extra years.  
• Earnings: Mincerian returns 6–10 % per extra year of schooling. Hence a 0.25-year gain translates into ~1.5–2.5 % higher wages.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1: Parallel pre-trends verified (event-study)……………………………… 1  
C2: Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)…………………………… 0.8  
C3: No anticipatory behavior or selective migration…………………… 0.7  
C4: Composition of cohorts stable (no differential mortality)……… 0.9  
C5: Correct standard-error clustering / inference……………………… 1  

Average ≈ 0.88 → high internal validity, but migration/ spillovers remain moderate concerns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan lays out a transparent DID design, diagnostics, and robustness steps to credibly estimate the causal impact of Indonesia’s massive primary-school build-out on later-life human-capital and labor-market outcomes.
